Populations of Anatolian khramulya in the Ceyhan River drainage exhibit a maximum recorded total length of 36 centimeters [Li = 36 centimeters], a value derived from extensive mark-recapture surveys conducted over a decade. This ultimate length is consistent with the upper range reported for other cyprinid species inhabiting similar Anatolian river systems, where prolonged growing seasons and adequate forage allow individuals to approach their asymptotic size. Field studies indicate that the total length at which puberty is attained is approximately 17 centimeters [Lp = approximately 17 centimeters], marking the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the transition to reproductive competence. The length-based maturation schedule appears to be shaped by local environmental conditions, with slower-growing individuals in upstream, cooler reaches reaching this milestone later in life compared to their counterparts in warmer, more productive downstream habitats. This pattern underscores the phenotypic plasticity inherent in the species' life history strategy.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Anatolian khramulya was assessed during the prespawning period. Under controlled laboratory conditions held at a stable 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the gonadosomatic index reached a mean value of 6% [GSI = 6%]. This level of investment is comparable to that observed in other iteroparous cyprinids that spawn annually, such as Capoeta capoeta, suggesting a conserved pattern of ovarian development within the genus. The GSI value was calculated from dissected females exhibiting fully vitellogenic oocytes, ensuring that the measurement represented peak reproductive condition prior to the spawning period. Such detailed physiological data are essential for parameterizing population models that aim to predict recruitment variability under shifting thermal regimes.

Neonatal body mass, a critical determinant of early survival and growth potential, has been estimated from the diameter of newly fertilized ova. Based on an average egg diameter of 1.6 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0021 grams [Wwb = 0.0021 grams], a value that assumes a spherical geometry and a density approximating that of freshwater. This minute starting mass places the yolk-sac larva in a vulnerable ecological position, as endogenous reserves must sustain the prolarva until the onset of exogenous feeding, a period typically lasting several days post-eclosion at 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. The relationship between egg size and larval fitness has been well documented in cyprinids, and the relatively small ova produced by Anatolian khramulya suggest a strategy favoring high fecundity over per-offspring investment.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by adult Anatolian khramulya, derived from the length-weight relationship established for the species, is approximately 433 grams [Wwi = approximately 433 grams]. This asymptotic mass is attained only by the oldest and largest individuals in the population, those that have successfully navigated the cumulative risks of predation and resource limitation over many growing seasons. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty, corresponding to the onset of reproductive activity at a total length of 17 centimeters, is roughly 47 grams [Wwp = roughly 47 grams]. This substantial difference between mass at maturation and maximum adult mass indicates an extended period of post-pubertal somatic growth, a life history pattern typical of iteroparous fishes that continue to increase fecundity with body size. The allometric coefficient used in the length-weight conversion, derived from a regional dataset, reinforces the robustness of these mass estimates.

Longevity data for Anatolian khramulya, compiled from otolith-based age assignments in the Ceyhan River system, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 6 years [am = approximately 6 years] under natural thermal conditions averaging 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This lifespan is within the range documented for other Capoeta species inhabiting temperate Anatolian streams, where seasonal productivity pulses and moderate metabolic demands associated with the regional climate contribute to a relatively extended life span compared to small-bodied cyprinids. Examination of annuli from the oldest individuals revealed narrow growth increments in the final years of life, consistent with the cessation of somatic investment as senescence approaches. The relationship between the stable thermal environment and the rate of physiological aging warrants further investigation, particularly given the potential for climate-driven shifts in growing season length to alter realized longevity and, consequently, lifetime reproductive output.
